Let $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =4\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡({x}^{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi /2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi $ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}5x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }5\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{5}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi }$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2\pi $ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(1-1) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(1/x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

If we let $u=4{x}^{2},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=8x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi /12}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /3$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /12}}8xsec\,(4{x}^{2})tan\,(4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /12}}sec\,(4{x}^{2})tan\,(4{x}^{2})\cdot 8x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=5{x}^{2},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=10x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\sqrt{\pi /30}$ | $\sqrt{\pi /10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /30}}^{\sqrt{\pi /10}}10xcsc\,(5{x}^{2})cot\,(5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /30}}^{\sqrt{\pi /10}}csc\,(5{x}^{2})cot\,(5{x}^{2})\cdot 10x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\operatorname{cot}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)) \\  & =-(1-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}{csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{csc}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\int {csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡({x}^{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{csc}⁡({x}^{2})\operatorname{cot}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡({x}^{2})\operatorname{cot}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡({x}^{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=4 x^{2}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=8 x.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - 16 x \csc^{2}{\left(4 x^{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-2\left(\int \csc^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-2\left(\int \csc^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=2 \cot{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
2 \cot{\left(4 x^{2} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=x^{3}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=3 x^{2}.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - 9 x^{2} \sin{\left(x^{3} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-3\left(\int \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-3\left(\int \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=3 \cos{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
3 \cos{\left(x^{3} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=4 x^{3}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=12 x^{2}.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - 12 x^{2} \sec^{2}{\left(4 x^{3} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-\int \sec^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-\int \sec^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u=- \tan{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- \tan{\left(4 x^{3} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=\frac{2}{x}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{x^{2}}.
$$

The negative derivative is included in the factor outside the new integral.

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - \frac{\sin{\left(\frac{2}{x} \right)}}{x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\int \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(\int \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=- \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{2}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- \frac{\cos{\left(\frac{2}{x} \right)}}{2}+C.
$$

Let $u=x^{2}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2 x.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - 2 x \cos{\left(x^{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-\int \cos{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-\int \cos{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u=- \sin{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- \sin{\left(x^{2} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=\frac{5}{x}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{5}{x^{2}}.
$$

The negative derivative is included in the factor outside the new integral.

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - \frac{2 \sec^{2}{\left(\frac{5}{x} \right)}}{x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\frac{2}{5}\left(\int \sec^{2}{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}

Substitute back:

$$
\frac{2 \tan{\left(\frac{5}{x} \right)}}{5}+C.
$$

Find an antiderivative.

\int - 9 x^{2} \tan{\left(3 x^{3} \right)} \sec{\left(3 x^{3} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=3 x^{3}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=9 x^{2}.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - 9 x^{2} \tan{\left(3 x^{3} \right)} \sec{\left(3 x^{3} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-\int \tan{\left(u \right)} \sec{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-\int \tan{\left(u \right)} \sec{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u=- \sec{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- \sec{\left(3 x^{3} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=3 x^{2} - \frac{\pi}{6}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=6 x.
$$

Change both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\sqrt{5} \sqrt{\pi}}{6}&\Longrightarrow u=\frac{\pi}{4}\\x=\frac{\sqrt{6} \sqrt{\pi}}{6}&\Longrightarrow u=\frac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{\frac{\sqrt{5} \sqrt{\pi}}{6}}^{\frac{\sqrt{6} \sqrt{\pi}}{6}} - 4 x \sin{\left(3 x^{2} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=- \frac{2}{3}\left(\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate and evaluate at both bounds:

$$
\left[\frac{2 \cos{\left(u \right)}}{3}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right).
$$

Simplifying gives

$$
\frac{1}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Let $u=2 \sqrt{x} - \frac{\pi}{6}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.
$$

Substituting, including the required constant factor, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int - \frac{2 \cos{\left(2 \sqrt{x} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-2\left(\int \cos{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-2\left(\int \cos{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=- 2 \sin{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- 2 \sin{\left(2 \sqrt{x} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}+C.
$$

Let $u=3 x^{3} - \frac{\pi}{4}$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=9 x^{2}.
$$

Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$
